results.title: How to Store AI Prompts: Build a Reusable Prompt Library | Snippety – Snippets Manager & Text Expander
results.content:
Prompts with variables take values positionally, in the order the placeholders appear, or pop the normal fill form:

`snippety expand pr-translate --var "Japanese" snippety expand pr-review --show-form # ask me for what I left out`

And `--in-app` sends the expanded text to whatever app is in front instead of back to the terminal, which is what makes prompts bindable to global hotkeys via a daemon like `skhd`. Details in the CLI documentation.

## Step 5: Let your AI agent fetch its own prompts [...] ### A text expander

This is the option most people overlook, and it maps almost exactly onto the five requirements above. A text expander stores blocks of text and inserts them when you type a keyword - system-wide, in any app. Prompts are blocks of text. The fit is not a coincidence: a prompt library is a snippet library where the snippets happen to be addressed to a model.

The rest of this guide uses Snippety for the examples, because it stores prompts locally, adds template variables, can call an AI model from inside a snippet, and exposes the whole library to the terminal. The general pattern applies to any capable expander.

## Step 1: Store each prompt as a snippet with a keyword [...] If you use AI daily, you have a private collection of prompts that work. The one that makes ChatGPT summarize a meeting the way you like. The one that gets Claude to review code without lecturing you. The system prompt you spent an hour tuning.

And you almost certainly cannot find any of them right now.

Storing AI prompts is a solved problem, but most people solve it badly - a scratch note, a pinned chat, a Slack message to themselves. This guide covers where to actually store prompts, what separates a real prompt library from a text dump, and how to make the library reachable everywhere you type: chat apps, your editor, the terminal, and even your coding agent.

results.title: Selected-Text AI Actions: Summarize, Rewrite, Explain, Translate | SideNote Pro
results.content:
The common thread is that the source application never loses focus for longer than the round trip. Which applications allow capture is set out under how capture works. See AI actions on selected text for the full walkthrough.

Selected-text actions work on text that already exists. For text you are still writing, inline commands do the job from inside the field: type a trigger such as `/fix` before the text, press Tab, and the result replaces it in place. For a message you are writing in your own language, `/en` translates it to English in the same field.

## How capture works, and its limits

Text capture happens only when you press the Selection actions shortcut or an action's own shortcut. SideNote Pro does not read the clipboard in the background and does not poll for selections. [...] SideNote Pro

# Run AI actions on text selected in Windows applications

The fastest AI interaction is the one with no copying, no pasting and no window switching. The AI comes to the text rather than you carrying the text to another application: select it in a Windows application, press `Ctrl+Shift+Q`, choose what to do, and the answer appears beside your work, ready to copy or, in supported editors, to put back where it came from. It works wherever an application lets SideNote Pro copy the selection. Password fields and applications running as administrator are the exceptions, and putting the answer back has its own rules, set out below. New to it? The step-by-step guide starts with your first action.
